1. Purpose
This policy says how Harbourlight Media clears advertising in the five restricted categories before it is transmitted:
alcohol, betting and gaming, less healthy food, consumer credit, and medicines and health. It says who reviews a
campaign, who decides it, what each decision means and what the agency is told.
It applies to every campaign in those categories booked on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight
Drama and Harbourlight Life, whichever scheduling system the channel uses.

2. Roles
 
Clearance Executive - works the clearance queue, reviews a campaign's copy and its booked spots, and writes
the clearance assessment with a recommended decision.
 
Clearance Controller - reads the assessment of a campaign they did not start, and decides the campaign. Only a
Clearance Controller may clear a campaign or withdraw a spot.
 
Legal Adviser - reviews a claim, an offer or a comparison when an executive asks, and records a legal review on
the campaign.
 
Agency Liaison - answers agencies' questions about the codes and about scheduling, and tells an agency the
status of its own campaigns.
Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes the forecast under-18 audience index

the
status of its own campaigns.
Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes the forecast under-18 audience index of every programme, as the
Scheduling and Audience Rules describe.

3. Separation of review and clearance
The executive who reviews a campaign may not clear it. Every campaign is decided by a Clearance Controller who
did not start its assessment, and the decision is recorded with the name of the Controller who took it and the reason,
in their own words.
A Controller who started a campaign's assessment has reviewed it, and may not decide it; another Controller must.
An assessment - however it was produced - is a recommendation. No spot is cleared, no spot is withdrawn and
nothing is sent to the agency until the decision is recorded. Tools may place and check every spot and draft the
documents, but clearing a campaign is never a machine's decision.

4. What is checked
Every campaign is checked in two parts:
1
The copy. The claims it makes, any offer and whether its terms are shown, the performers, and everything the
category's code says the copy must or must not do. The executive reads the notes on the campaign - the first
read, any legal review, the agency's replies and any update - and the issue guide for the issue they raise.
2
The booked spots. Every spot is placed on its broadcast day, in or adjacent to the programmes around its break,
and tested against the scheduling rules of the category's own code: restricted hours, the under-18 audience,
programmes made for children, the daily limit and the separation.
Each category's rules

hours, the under-18 audience,
programmes made for children, the daily limit and the separation.
Each category's rules are read from its own code and from no other document. The five codes share one layout and
many of the same sentences. They differ in their figures, in the children's rule, which the medicines and health code
applies only in a programme made for children, and in one exception that only the betting and gaming code has.

5. The three decisions
The Controller chooses one of three decisions, each open only as set out here:
 
CLEAR - every booked spot is cleared. Open only when no spot breaks the code.
 
CLEAR WITH RESTRICTIONS - the compliant spots are cleared and the spots that break the code are
withdrawn. Open only when at least one spot breaks the code and at least one does not.
 
REJECT - no spot is cleared. Always open, whatever the spots' results, for example when the copy cannot be
cleared.
A decision the spots do not allow is refused: CLEAR while any spot breaks the code, and CLEAR WITH
RESTRICTIONS when no spot breaks the code or when no spot complies.
The campaign's record moves from pending a

WITH
RESTRICTIONS when no spot breaks the code or when no spot complies.
The campaign's record moves from pending a decision to cleared, cleared with restrictions or rejected, and keeps the
assessment, the decision, the reason, the spots cleared and withdrawn, and every document sent.

6. The restriction notice
When a campaign is cleared with restrictions, the agency is sent a restriction notice before the certificate is issued.
The notice is written for the agency: plain words, each withdrawn spot once with its channel, broadcast day and time
and every rule it broke, and what to do next, taken from the section of the campaign's own code on re-booking a
withdrawn spot.
It must never contain the internal assessment, a model's score, a note, the name of an executive or a Controller, or
another agency's name.

7. The clearance certificate
A campaign that is cleared, with or without restrictions, is issued a clearance certificate. It must show:
 
the campaign reference, the clock number, the advertiser and the product category
 
each cleared spot on its own line, with its spot reference, channel, broadcast day and broadcast time
 
no withdrawn spot, and no cleared spot twice
 
the standing restrictions the category's code places on every cleared spot
 
where a restriction notice was sent, a line saying the agency has been sent it
Every spot, time and rule on the certificate and on the notice is taken from the spot checks; none is worked out again
by hand.

8. When a campaign is rejected
A rejected campaign is issued neither a certificate nor a notice. The Controller's reason is recorded, and the agency
may submit the copy again, amended where it needs to be, as a new campaign.

9. The order campaigns are worked in
Campaigns are worked in order of their exposure: the under-18 audience their non-compliant spots would reach. For
each spot that breaks the code, the forecast of under-18 viewers for the programme it is in is taken - or, for a spot in
an end break, the larger of the two programmes' forecasts. The figures are added up for the campaign, in thousands,
and the total is rounded once to one decimal place.
The largest exposure comes first. Between campaigns with the same exposure, the one whose first spot is
transmitted earlier in the booking week comes first, and campaigns that still tie are taken in alphabetical order of
campaign reference.
Each campaign's

week comes first, and campaigns that still tie are taken in alphabetical order of
campaign reference.
Each campaign's copy is also given an amendment score, the likelihood that the copy will need changes before it can
be cleared. The score is shown to four decimal places and banded on the figure shown: HIGH from 0.60, MEDIUM
from 0.30 and LOW below that.

10. Talking to agencies about a campaign
An Agency Liaison tells an agency about its own campaigns only - those of the agencies assigned to the liaison.
Before a decision they give the status and when it last changed; after it, the decision, how many spots were cleared
and withdrawn, and which documents the agency has been sent.
They never give a model's score, an index, a note or anything from the assessment.
A campaign booked by an agency that is not assigned to the liaison is treated as though it did not exist: the liaison
says it cannot be found, in the same words used for a reference that does not exist. Agencies compete for the same
airtime, and a campaign is confidential between its

airtime, and a campaign is confidential between its agency and Harbourlight.
Questions about the codes and about the Scheduling and Audience Rules are answered for anyone, because the
codes are published to agencies.

1. Purpose and scope
This code sets out when and where Harbourlight Media may transmit advertising for alcoholic drinks. It applies to
every spot of every campaign in the category on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight Drama and
Harbourlight Life.
A campaign is cleared in full only when its copy is acceptable and every booked spot meets the scheduling rules in
sections 4 to 7; when some spots do not, only its compliant spots can be cleared. The clearance desk checks both,
and a Clearance Controller decides, as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes.
The code is published to agencies and may be quoted to anyone who asks.

2. Products covered
This code covers advertising for alcoholic drinks: beer and lager, cider, wine, spirits and ready-to-drink cocktails.
It also covers advertising for an alcohol-free drink sold under the same brand name as an alcoholic drink.

3. How this code is applied
The rules in sections 4 to 7 apply to every booked spot of a campaign for alcoholic drinks, on the broadcast day the
spot belongs to.
Times in this code are written on the ordinary 24-hour clock. The Scheduling and Audience Rules explain how they
are placed on the broadcast day, and what a centre break, an end break, in and adjacent mean.
A spot in a centre break is in the programme around it. A spot in an end break is adjacent to the programme before it
and to the programme after it.
A spot that meets every rule may be transmitted. A spot that breaks a rule may not be transmitted, and is recorded
against every rule it breaks.

4. Restricted hours
Spots for this category may be transmitted at any time of the broadcast day.
The rules in sections 5 to 7 still apply to every spot.

5. The under-18 audience
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme whose under-18 audience index is 120 or more.
The index is the forecast under-18 audience index that Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes for each
programme before the booking week begins, as the programme schedule shows it.
A spot in an end break is tested against both programmes, and breaks this rule if either of them is indexed at or
above the figure in this section.

6. Programmes made for children
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme made for children.
A programme is made for children when the programme schedule marks it so, whatever its under-18 audience index.
The rule covers the end breaks before and after such a programme as well as its centre breaks.

7. How many spots, and how far apart
No more than 6 spots of one campaign may be transmitted on one channel in one broadcast day.
Two spots of one campaign on one channel must be at least 20 minutes apart.
Both rules are applied per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day, to the spots in the order they are
transmitted. Every booked spot counts towards the limit, whether or not it breaks another rule.
The separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day. Two
spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart and are transmitted in the order of their spot references.

8. Copy requirements
The copy of every campaign in this category must meet these requirements, and the issue guides say how the
clearance desk checks each kind of claim.
 
The copy must not link drinking with popularity, confidence, social or sexual success, or daring.
 
No one who is, or looks, under 25 may be shown drinking or play a significant role.
 
The copy must not show or suggest drinking to excess, or drinking before driving, swimming or working with
machinery.
 
The copy must not appeal strongly to under-18s through its characters, music, humour or setting.
 
A statement of low calories or low alcohol must use the permitted wording, and no other health claim may be
made.

9. Standing restrictions on every cleared spot
Every cleared spot in this category is cleared subject to these standing restrictions:
 
A cleared spot may be transmitted only on the channel, broadcast day and break its certificate shows.
 
The copy is cleared as submitted under its clock number, and any change needs a new clearance.
 
If a programme's forecast index is revised before transmission, a spot in or adjacent to it must be checked again
against section 5.
 
The spot may not be transmitted next to a programme item about drink-driving or alcohol harm.

10. Re-booking a withdrawn spot
This category has no restricted hours, so a spot withdrawn under section 5 or section 6 needs a break whose
programmes are forecast below the threshold in section 5 and are not made for children. Such breaks are found most
often later in the evening, when fewer under-18s are watching. A spot withdrawn under section 7 may move to
another broadcast day or channel, where it counts with the campaign's other spots there. Send the new break to the
clearance desk with the campaign and spot references, and the desk checks it against this code before it is
transmitted.

11. Questions about this code
Agencies can ask about the alcohol code through the Agency Liaison assigned to them. Questions about a particular
campaign are answered only for the agency that booked it.

1. Purpose and scope
This code sets out when and where Harbourlight Media may transmit advertising for betting and gaming. It applies to
every spot of every campaign in the category on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight Drama and
Harbourlight Life.
A campaign is cleared in full only when its copy is acceptable and every booked spot meets the scheduling rules in
sections 4 to 7; when some spots do not, only its compliant spots can be cleared. The clearance desk checks both,
and a Clearance Controller decides, as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes.
The code is published to agencies and may be quoted to anyone who asks.

2. Products covered
This code covers advertising for betting and gaming: sports betting, online casino, bingo, lottery and poker.
It also covers advertising for a free-to-play game offered under the brand of a betting or gaming business.

3. How this code is applied
The rules in sections 4 to 7 apply to every booked spot of a campaign for betting and gaming, on the broadcast day
the spot belongs to.
Times in this code are written on the ordinary 24-hour clock. The Scheduling and Audience Rules explain how they
are placed on the broadcast day, and what a centre break, an end break, in and adjacent mean.
A spot in a centre break is in the programme around it. A spot in an end break is adjacent to the programme before it
and to the programme after it.
A spot that meets every rule may be transmitted. A spot that breaks a rule may not be transmitted, and is recorded
against every rule it breaks.

4. Restricted hours
Spots for this category may not be transmitted between 05:30 and 21:00.
The restricted hours do not apply to a centre break within live sport coverage that begins more than 10 minutes after
the coverage starts and more than 10 minutes before it ends.
An end break is never within live sport coverage, and each live sport programme is its own coverage.

5. The under-18 audience
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme whose under-18 audience index is 110 or more.
The index is the forecast under-18 audience index that Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes for each
programme before the booking week begins, as the programme schedule shows it.
A spot in an end break is tested against both programmes, and breaks this rule if either of them is indexed at or
above the figure in this section.

6. Programmes made for children
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme made for children.
A programme is made for children when the programme schedule marks it so, whatever its under-18 audience index.
The rule covers the end breaks before and after such a programme as well as its centre breaks.

7. How many spots, and how far apart
No more than 7 spots of one campaign may be transmitted on one channel in one broadcast day.
Two spots of one campaign on one channel must be at least 30 minutes apart.
Both rules are applied per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day, to the spots in the order they are
transmitted. Every booked spot counts towards the limit, whether or not it breaks another rule.
The separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day. Two
spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart and are transmitted in the order of their spot references.

8. Copy requirements
The copy of every campaign in this category must meet these requirements, and the issue guides say how the
clearance desk checks each kind of claim.
 
An offer of a free bet, a bonus or a boosted price must show its significant terms with the headline, including the
minimum stake, the eligible markets and any wagering requirement.
 
The copy must not urge viewers to bet now, or suggest that an offer or a chance to win will be lost if they wait.
 
The copy must not present gambling as a way to solve money worries or to win approval, or suggest that skill will
beat the odds.
 
No one who is, or looks, under 25 may be shown gambling or play a significant role, and no

skill will
beat the odds.
 
No one who is, or looks, under 25 may be shown gambling or play a significant role, and no person or character
with strong appeal to under-18s may feature.
 
The safer gambling message must be on screen for the whole of the spot.

9. Standing restrictions on every cleared spot
Every cleared spot in this category is cleared subject to these standing restrictions:
 
A cleared spot may be transmitted only on the channel, broadcast day and break its certificate shows.
 
The copy is cleared as submitted under its clock number, and any change needs a new clearance.
 
If a programme's forecast index is revised before transmission, a spot in or adjacent to it must be checked again
against section 5.
 
A spot cleared within live sport coverage is cleared for that programme only, and must be checked again if the
coverage moves.
 
The spot may not be transmitted next to a programme item about problem gambling.

10. Re-booking a withdrawn spot
Move a spot withdrawn under section 4 to a break outside the restricted hours, or to a centre break of live sport
coverage that the exception in section 4 allows. Where the new break is an end break, check both programmes
against section 5, because a programme straight after a live match is often forecast at a high index. A spot withdrawn
under section 7 may move to another broadcast day or channel, where it counts with the campaign's other spots
there. Send the new break to the clearance desk with the campaign and spot references, and the desk checks it
against this code before it is transmitted.

11. Questions about this code
Agencies can ask about the betting and gaming code through the Agency Liaison assigned to them. Questions about
a particular campaign are answered only for the agency that booked it.

1. Purpose and scope
This code sets out when and where Harbourlight Media may transmit advertising for consumer credit. It applies to
every spot of every campaign in the category on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight Drama and
Harbourlight Life.
A campaign is cleared in full only when its copy is acceptable and every booked spot meets the scheduling rules in

and a Clearance Controller decides, as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes.
The code is published to agencies and may be quoted to anyone who asks.

2. Products covered
This code covers advertising for consumer credit: credit cards, personal loans, buy now pay later plans, car finance
and short-term loans.
It also covers advertising by a broker or a comparison service that introduces viewers to consumer credit.

3. How this code is applied
The rules in sections 4 to 7 apply to every booked spot of a campaign for consumer credit, on the broadcast day the
spot belongs to.
Times in this code are written on the ordinary 24-hour clock. The Scheduling and Audience Rules explain how they
are placed on the broadcast day, and what a centre break, an end break, in and adjacent mean.
A spot in a centre break is in the programme around it. A spot in an end break is adjacent to the programme before it
and to the programme after it.
A spot that meets every rule may be transmitted. A spot that breaks a rule may not be transmitted, and is recorded
against every rule it breaks.

4. Restricted hours
Spots for this category may not be transmitted between 06:00 and 19:00.
The restricted hours apply to every break, including a break within live sport coverage.

5. The under-18 audience
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme whose under-18 audience index is 125 or more.
The index is the forecast under-18 audience index that Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes for each
programme before the booking week begins, as the programme schedule shows it.
A spot in an end break is tested against both programmes, and breaks this rule if either of them is indexed at or
above the figure in this section.

6. Programmes made for children
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme made for children.
A programme is made for children when the programme schedule marks it so, whatever its under-18 audience index.
The rule covers the end breaks before and after such a programme as well as its centre breaks.

7. How many spots, and how far apart
No more than 5 spots of one campaign may be transmitted on one channel in one broadcast day.
Two spots of one campaign on one channel must be at least 15 minutes apart.
Both rules are applied per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day, to the spots in the order they are
transmitted. Every booked spot counts towards the limit, whether or not it breaks another rule.
The separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day. Two
spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart and are transmitted in the order of their spot references.

8. Copy requirements
The copy of every campaign in this category must meet these requirements, and the issue guides say how the
clearance desk checks each kind of claim.
 
Copy that states an interest rate, a repayment, an interest-free period or any other figure about the cost of credit
must show the representative APR and the representative example, at least as prominently as that figure.
 
The copy must not claim that credit is guaranteed, available without checks, or approved in minutes.
 
The copy must not urge viewers to borrow now, or present borrowing as a way out of money worries.
 
Copy for a buy now pay later plan must say that missed repayments can affect a credit rating.

of money worries.
 
Copy for a buy now pay later plan must say that missed repayments can affect a credit rating.
 
Copy for a short-term loan must carry the risk warning about the cost of short-term borrowing.

9. Standing restrictions on every cleared spot
Every cleared spot in this category is cleared subject to these standing restrictions:
 
A cleared spot may be transmitted only on the channel, broadcast day and break its certificate shows.
 
The copy is cleared as submitted under its clock number, and any change needs a new clearance.
 
If a programme's forecast index is revised before transmission, a spot in or adjacent to it must be checked again
against section 5.
 
The representative APR must stay on screen for as long as any cost of credit is shown or spoken.

10. Re-booking a withdrawn spot
Move a spot withdrawn under section 4 to a break outside the restricted hours, usually in the evening. A break that
begins at the moment the restricted hours end is outside them and may be used. A spot withdrawn under section 7
may move to another broadcast day or channel, where it counts with the campaign's other spots there. Send the new
break to the clearance desk with the campaign and spot references, and the desk checks it against this code before it
is transmitted.

11. Questions about this code
Agencies can ask about the consumer credit code through the Agency Liaison assigned to them. Questions about a
particular campaign are answered only for the agency that booked it.

1. Purpose and scope
This code sets out when and where Harbourlight Media may transmit advertising for less healthy food and drink. It
applies to every spot of every campaign in the category on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight Drama

and a Clearance Controller decides, as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes.
The code is published to agencies and may be quoted to anyone who asks.

2. Products covered
This code covers advertising for less healthy food and drink: confectionery, soft drinks, fast food, savoury snacks,
breakfast cereals and ice cream that Harbourlight's nutrient profiling assessment identifies as less healthy.
A product the assessment does not identify as less healthy is not advertised under this code.

3. How this code is applied
The rules in sections 4 to 7 apply to every booked spot of a campaign for less healthy food and drink, on the
broadcast day the spot belongs to.
Times in this code are written on the ordinary 24-hour clock. The Scheduling and Audience Rules explain how they
are placed on the broadcast day, and what a centre break, an end break, in and adjacent mean.
A spot in a centre break is in the programme around it. A spot in an end break is adjacent to the programme before it
and to the programme after it.
A spot that meets every rule may be transmitted. A spot that breaks a rule may not be transmitted, and is recorded
against every rule it breaks.

4. Restricted hours
Spots for this category may not be transmitted between 05:30 and 21:00.
The restricted hours apply to every break, including a break within live sport coverage.

5. The under-18 audience
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme whose under-18 audience index is 120 or more.
The index is the forecast under-18 audience index that Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes for each
programme before the booking week begins, as the programme schedule shows it.
A spot in an end break is tested against both programmes, and breaks this rule if either of them is indexed at or
above the figure in this section.

6. Programmes made for children
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme made for children.
A programme is made for children when the programme schedule marks it so, whatever its under-18 audience index.
The rule covers the end breaks before and after such a programme as well as its centre breaks.

7. How many spots, and how far apart
No more than 8 spots of one campaign may be transmitted on one channel in one broadcast day.
Two spots of one campaign on one channel must be at least 10 minutes apart.
Both rules are applied per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day, to the spots in the order they are
transmitted. Every booked spot counts towards the limit, whether or not it breaks another rule.
The separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day. Two
spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart and are transmitted in the order of their spot references.

8. Copy requirements
The copy of every campaign in this category must meet these requirements, and the issue guides say how the
clearance desk checks each kind of claim.
 
A health or nutrition claim may be made only when the product meets the conditions for it, in the permitted
wording.
 
The copy must not use a character, a celebrity or a licensed property with strong appeal to under-18s to promote
the product.
 
The copy must not offer a promotion, a collectable or a giveaway aimed at under-18s.
 
The copy must not encourage eating or drinking to excess, or suggest that the product can take the place of a
balanced diet.
 
A price or an offer must be genuine, with its significant

that the product can take the place of a
balanced diet.
 
A price or an offer must be genuine, with its significant conditions on screen beside the headline.

9. Standing restrictions on every cleared spot
Every cleared spot in this category is cleared subject to these standing restrictions:
 
A cleared spot may be transmitted only on the channel, broadcast day and break its certificate shows.
 
The copy is cleared as submitted under its clock number, and any change needs a new clearance.
 
If a programme's forecast index is revised before transmission, a spot in or adjacent to it must be checked again
against section 5.
 
The copy may not be cut down, or used as a programme sponsorship credit, without a new clearance.

10. Re-booking a withdrawn spot
Move a spot withdrawn under section 4 to a break outside the restricted hours. This code has no exception for live
sport coverage, so a break inside a live match during the restricted hours is no alternative. Late evening breaks next
to programmes forecast below the threshold in section 5 are the usual choice. A spot withdrawn under section 7 may
move to another broadcast day or channel, where it counts with the campaign's other spots there. Send the new
break to the clearance desk with the campaign and spot references, and the desk checks it against this code before it
is transmitted.

11. Questions about this code
Agencies can ask about the less healthy food code through the Agency Liaison assigned to them. Questions about a
particular campaign are answered only for the agency that booked it.

1. Purpose and scope
This code sets out when and where Harbourlight Media may transmit advertising for medicines and health products.
It applies to every spot of every campaign in the category on Harbourlight One, Harbourlight Sport, Harbourlight
Drama and Harbourlight Life.
A campaign is cleared in full only when its copy is acceptable and every booked spot meets the scheduling rules in
sections 4 to 7; when some spots do not, only its compliant spots can be cleared. The clearance desk checks both,
and a Clearance Controller decides, as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes.
The code is published to agencies and may be quoted to anyone who asks.

2. Products covered
This code covers advertising for medicines and health products sold without a prescription: pain relief, cold and flu
remedies, allergy relief, vitamins and supplements, digestive health products and sleep aids.
Medicines available only on prescription may not be advertised on Harbourlight's channels.

3. How this code is applied
The rules in sections 4 to 7 apply to every booked spot of a campaign for medicines and health products, on the
broadcast day the spot belongs to.
Times in this code are written on the ordinary 24-hour clock. The Scheduling and Audience Rules explain how they
are placed on the broadcast day, and what a centre break, an end break, in and adjacent mean.
A spot in a centre break is in the programme around it. A spot in an end break is adjacent to the programme before it
and to the programme after it.
A spot that meets every rule may be transmitted. A spot that breaks a rule may not be transmitted, and is recorded
against every rule it breaks.

4. Restricted hours
Spots for this category may be transmitted at any time of the broadcast day.
The rules in sections 5 to 7 still apply to every spot.

5. The under-18 audience
Spots may not be transmitted in or adjacent to a programme whose under-18 audience index is 150 or more.
The index is the forecast under-18 audience index that Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes for each
programme before the booking week begins, as the programme schedule shows it.
A spot in an end break is tested against both programmes, and breaks this rule if either of them is indexed at or
above the figure in this section.

6. Programmes made for children
Spots may not be transmitted in a programme made for children.
A programme is made for children when the programme schedule marks it so, whatever its under-18 audience index.
The rule covers the centre breaks of such a programme only. A spot in an end break next to it is not caught by this
rule, but must still meet section 5.

7. How many spots, and how far apart
No more than 10 spots of one campaign may be transmitted on one channel in one broadcast day.
Two spots of one campaign on one channel must be at least 5 minutes apart.
Both rules are applied per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day, to the spots in the order they are
transmitted. Every booked spot counts towards the limit, whether or not it breaks another rule.
The separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day. Two
spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart and are transmitted in the order of their spot references.

8. Copy requirements
The copy of every campaign in this category must meet these requirements, and the issue guides say how the
clearance desk checks each kind of claim.
 
Every claim about what the product does must be supported by evidence the advertiser holds, and must stay
within the product's licence.
 
The copy must not suggest that the product is certain to work, works faster than its evidence shows, or has no
side effects.
 
The copy must not show a doctor, a nurse or a presenter styled as one recommending the product.
 
The copy must not be addressed to under-18s, or show a child taking the product without an adult.
 
The copy must end with an on-screen line telling viewers to read

or show a child taking the product without an adult.
 
The copy must end with an on-screen line telling viewers to read the label.

9. Standing restrictions on every cleared spot
Every cleared spot in this category is cleared subject to these standing restrictions:
 
A cleared spot may be transmitted only on the channel, broadcast day and break its certificate shows.
 
The copy is cleared as submitted under its clock number, and any change needs a new clearance.
 
If a programme's forecast index is revised before transmission, a spot in or adjacent to it must be checked again
against section 5.
 
The line telling viewers to read the label must be on screen when the product is named at the end of the spot.

10. Re-booking a withdrawn spot
This category has no restricted hours, and its spots may be transmitted next to a programme made for children but
never in one. A spot withdrawn from a centre break of such a programme can often move to the end break before or
after it, provided both programmes are forecast below the threshold in section 5. A spot withdrawn under section 7
may move to another broadcast day or channel, where it counts with the campaign's other spots there. Send the new
break to the clearance desk with the campaign and spot references, and the desk checks it against this code before it
is transmitted.

11. Questions about this code
Agencies can ask about the medicines and health code through the Agency Liaison assigned to them. Questions
about a particular campaign are answered only for the agency that booked it.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers alcohol copy that links drinking with popularity, confidence, social or sexual success, or daring. It is
used by the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency
Liaisons advising agencies before they submit.
It arises in alcohol copy only.
This guide is about what the drink is shown to do. A performer who is, or looks, under 25 is an appeal to under-18s,
and the Appeal to Under-18s guide covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
the drinker becoming the life of the party or the centre of attention after a drink
 
a round of drinks turning someone into the most popular person in the room
 
a group that only starts having fun once the drinks arrive
 
confidence to take the stage, or a daring stunt, straight after drinking
 
the drink shown as the key to a great night out

3. What the executive checks
For a possible link between drinking and social success, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
Watch the copy scene by scene and note where the drink appears against any change in a character's mood or
standing.
2
Decide whether the drink causes the success in the story or is incidental to a scene of friends meeting.
3
Check that no line or super credits the drink with confidence, popularity, attraction or courage.
4
Check the copy does not show drinking to excess, or drinking linked with daring, driving or danger.
5
Ask for the storyboard when the order of the scenes decides the question.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the storyboard and the edit showing the order of the scenes
 
the script, with every line and super

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once the drink is incidental to any social scene and nothing suggests it brings confidence,
popularity or success. The usual amendment is to cut the moment a character is cheered or transformed after
drinking, or the line that links the two.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Show friends enjoying each other's company, with the drink incidental.
 
Avoid any change in a character that follows the drink.
 
Keep lines and supers from crediting the drink with confidence or popularity.
 
Send the storyboard with the copy.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when the agency argues that the scene shows friends meeting rather than the drink causing
the fun.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers copy that is likely to appeal particularly to people under 18. It is used by the Clearance Executive
who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency Liaisons advising agencies before
they submit.
It arises most often in less healthy food, alcohol and betting and gaming copy. No restricted category may aim its
copy at under-18s.
This guide is about who the copy speaks to. Copy that pressures viewers to gamble or promises winning is a
gambling inducement, and the Gambling Inducements guide covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code.

covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
a cartoon mascot, animated characters, video-game style graphics or a playground-style jingle
 
toy giveaways and collectable stickers
 
performers who are, or look, young - for alcohol and betting, anyone who looks under 25
 
sports personalities and celebrities with a strong following among young fans
 
school settings, and children shown enjoying the product

3. What the executive checks
For a possible appeal to under-18s, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
List every element likely to appeal to under-18s: characters, graphics, music, giveaways, settings and
performers.
2
For alcohol and betting, check every performer in a significant role is, and looks, 25 or over, and ask for their
ages.
3
Judge the copy as a whole: whether its treatment, not only one element, is aimed at a young audience.
4
Check that any sports personality or celebrity does not have a strong following among under-18s.
5
Keep this apart from scheduling: where the spots are booked cannot make such copy acceptable.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the performers' ages for alcohol and betting copy
 
the storyboard showing how each scene plays
 
for a celebrity or a sports personality, the profile of their following

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once nothing in it has particular appeal to under-18s and, for alcohol and betting, every
performer in a significant role is, and looks, 25 or over. The usual amendment is to remove the youth-facing element
or to recast with an older performer.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Leave out cartoons, toys, collectables and playground settings for these categories.
 
Cast performers who are, and look, 25 or over for alcohol and betting.
 
Send the performers' ages with the copy.
 
Check a celebrity's following before building the copy around them.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when the agency argues that the treatment is aimed at adults, or when a celebrity's appeal to
young fans is disputed.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers claims that compare a product with a competitor or with the rest of the market. It is used by the
Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency Liaisons
advising agencies before they submit.
It arises in all five categories: medicines said to work faster, credit said to be rated higher, food and drink said to taste
better or to sell more.
A claim about what a product does for health, with nothing to compare it with, is a health claim, and the Health Claims
guide covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is

Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
rankings such as number one in Britain or outsells every competitor
 
claims to beat the leading brand or to be twice as effective as the rest
 
a side-by-side shot with a rival product
 
preferred or rated higher, without saying by whom or on what measure

3. What the executive checks
For a comparative claim, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
Identify what is compared, with what, and on what measure.
2
Check the comparison is like with like: the same kind of product, the same period and the same market.
3
Check the competitor is identifiable, or that a comparison with the whole market is covered by the evidence.
4
Ask for the data or the independent test behind any objective claim, and check it is current.
5
Check that a named or shown competitor is represented fairly and not denigrated.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the sales data or the market share figures, and the period they cover
 
independent test results and the method used
 
for medicines, head-to-head evidence against the product compared

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once the comparison is like with like, current, verifiable and fair. The usual amendment is to
narrow the claim to what the evidence shows, such as preferred in an independent test in place of a ranking, with the
basis on screen.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
State the basis of the comparison on screen.
 
Keep rankings to what current data for the same market and period show.
 
Send the data and the test method with the copy.
 
Show competitors fairly.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when a competitor is named or shown, or when a claim rests on the advertiser's own research.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers claims that a product, its packaging or the business behind it is better for the environment. It is
used by the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency
Liaisons advising agencies before they submit.
It arises most often in less healthy food and alcohol copy about packaging, and now and then in betting, credit and
medicines copy about how a business is run.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
absolute wording such as eco-friendly, carbon neutral or zero waste
 
packaging described as fully recyclable, plastic-free or made from recycled materials
 
planet imagery that implies a benefit the copy does not state
 
a claim about one part of a product presented as true of the whole

3. What the executive checks
For an environmental claim, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
Identify every environmental claim, whether spoken, written or implied by the images.
2
Ask which part of the product, the pack or the business each claim covers, and check the copy says so.
3
Check any absolute claim is backed by evidence covering the whole product and its full life cycle.
4
Ask for independent verification of carbon neutral, recyclable and similar claims.
5
Check that any qualification is on screen with the claim, not left to a website.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
recycling certificates for each part of the pack
 
an independent verification or a sustainability report
 
the basis of any carbon claim, and whether it relies on offsetting

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once each claim states exactly what it covers and the evidence supports it for the whole of
that part. The usual amendment is to qualify the line - which part is recyclable, or what is carbon neutral and on what
basis - or to remove absolute wording.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Say exactly which part of the product or the pack a claim covers.
 
Avoid absolute wording unless the evidence covers the whole life cycle.
 
Send certificates and verification with the copy.
 
Make sure the images promise no more than the words.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when a claim relies on offsetting, when the verification is not independent, or when the agency
maintains an unqualified claim.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers consumer credit copy that states or implies what credit costs, or how easy it is to get. It is used by
the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency Liaisons
advising agencies before they submit.
It arises in consumer credit copy: credit cards, personal loans, buy now pay later plans, car finance and short-term
loans.
This guide is about what credit costs, including a 0% or interest-free period, and how easily it is given. A gift, a
voucher or cashback offered with a credit product is a price or offer claim, and the Price and Offer Claims guide
covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may

credit product is a price or offer claim, and the Price and Offer Claims guide
covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
a monthly repayment, a low weekly figure, an interest-free period or a rate of 0% for a set number of months
 
a representative APR that is missing, or much smaller than the repayment figure
 
guaranteed approval, no credit checks or approval in minutes
 
a pay-later plan that does not say missed repayments can affect a credit rating
 
a short-term loan without the risk warning

3. What the executive checks
For a financial promotion, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
List every figure about the cost of credit the copy states, whether spoken or written.
2
Check that any such figure brings in the representative APR and the representative example, shown at least as
prominently.
3
Check the total amount repayable is clear wherever the representative example is required.
4
Check that nothing suggests credit is guaranteed or given without affordability checks.
5
For pay-later plans, check the credit rating statement; for short-term loans, the risk warning.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the lender's representative example
 
the representative APR and how it was worked out
 
the lender's approval criteria, for any claim about approval

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once every figure about the cost of credit is shown with the representative APR and the
representative example, at least as prominently as the figure, and nothing overstates how easily credit is given. The
usual amendment is to add the representative APR and the total amount repayable to the end frame.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Show the representative APR and the representative example whenever any cost figure appears.
 
Give them at least the prominence of the most prominent cost figure.
 
Remove claims of guaranteed approval or of no checks.
 
Send the lender's representative example with the copy.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when a figure may bring in the representative example, or when the agency says the rate
shown is the one most customers get.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers betting and gaming copy that pressures viewers to gamble or misleads them about what gambling
offers. It is used by the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by
Agency Liaisons advising agencies before they submit.
It arises in betting and gaming copy only.
This guide is about what the copy promises and how it pushes viewers to act. Copy aimed at a young audience is an
appeal to under-18s, and the Appeal to Under-18s guide covers it; an offer's terms, and whether they are shown, are
a price or offer claim.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the

shown, are
a price or offer claim.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
urgency, such as bet now before kick-off, get in before the odds change or sign up today and play straight away
 
a 'today only' super
 
a win shown as the answer to money worries
 
a player doubling a stake after a loss, which looks like chasing losses
 
a suggestion that skill will beat the odds, or that everyone watching the match is betting

3. What the executive checks
For a possible gambling inducement, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
List every line and image that urges viewers to gamble now or suggests an offer will be lost if they wait.
2
Check the copy does not present gambling as a way to solve money worries, gain status or win approval.
3
Check that no scene shows chasing losses or gambling beyond a player's means.
4
Check the copy is not misleading about the chance of winning and does not suggest skill will beat the odds.
5
Check the safer gambling message is on screen for the whole of the spot.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the script notes explaining any winning scene
 
where the copy says a winner is a real customer, confirmation of it
 
the full terms of any offer shown

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once it no longer pressures viewers to gamble, presents winning realistically and carries the
safer gambling message throughout. The usual amendment is to remove the urgency line and any winning montage.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Remove lines that urge viewers to bet or play now.
 
Show winning as occasional, and gambling as entertainment rather than a way out of money worries.
 
Keep the safer gambling message on screen for the whole spot.
 
Send script notes for any scene that shows a win.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when the agency says a winning scene is real and typical, or when urgency is implied by the
images rather than the words.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers claims that a product benefits health, relieves a condition or has a nutritional quality. It is used by
the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled, and by Agency Liaisons
advising agencies before they submit.
It arises most often in medicines and health copy, and in less healthy food copy that describes the product as healthy
or nutritious. Alcohol copy may state low calories only in the permitted wording.
A claim that the product works better or faster than another product is a comparative claim, and the Comparative
Claims guide covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a

is a comparative claim, and the Comparative
Claims guide covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
a voiceover or a super saying what the product does for the body - relieves, clears, boosts, fights or protects
 
an onset time or a length of effect, such as relief in minutes or protection all day
 
'clinically proven', a trial result, or a presenter styled as a doctor
 
nutrition wording on food or drink, such as full of goodness, high in fibre or a lighter choice
 
low calorie or fewer calories on alcohol

3. What the executive checks
For a health or nutrition claim, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
Write down every health or nutrition claim in the voiceover, the supers and the pack shot.
2
For a medicine, check each claim against the product's licence: the licensed indication, the dose and any onset
time.
3
For food and drink, check the product meets the nutrient conditions and the wording is in the permitted form.
4
Ask for evidence behind any claim the licence or the nutrient conditions do not cover, and hold the copy until it
arrives.
5
Check that no presenter styled as a doctor endorses the product and nothing suggests it is certain to work.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the product licence and the product's summary of characteristics
 
trial results for any onset time or length of effect
 
the nutrient analysis for a claim on food or drink
 
the permitted wording for a nutrition claim

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once every claim is covered by the licence, the nutrient conditions or evidence on file, in
wording no stronger than the evidence. The usual amendment is to soften a claim to the permitted wording, such as
helps relieve in place of a cure, or to drop it.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Send the licence, the trial data or the nutrient analysis with the copy, not after the first read.
 
Use the permitted wording for nutrition claims and the licensed wording for medicines.
 
Keep onset times and lengths of effect to what the evidence states.
 
Leave out endorsements by doctors or by presenters styled as doctors.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when a claim goes beyond the licence, when the evidence is a single study, or when the
agency disputes that the wording is a health claim at all.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. What this guide covers
This guide covers claims about a product's price and offers such as savings, multibuys, boosted odds, free bets and
cashback. It is used by the Clearance Executive who reviews the copy, from the first read until the issue is settled,
and by Agency Liaisons advising agencies before they submit.
It arises most often in less healthy food, betting and gaming and alcohol copy, and in any category that runs a
promotion.
A gift, a voucher or cashback offered with a credit product is a price or offer claim, but any figure about what credit
costs - an APR, a repayment, or a 0% or interest-free period - is a financial promotion, and the Financial Promotions
guide covers it.

a repayment, or a 0% or interest-free period - is a financial promotion, and the Financial Promotions
guide covers it. A betting offer pushed with urgency is a gambling inducement, and the Gambling Inducements guide
covers it.
Whether a campaign's spots may be transmitted is a separate question, settled by the category's own code. This
guide is about the copy.

2. How it usually shows up
 
a headline saving: half price, two for one, a meal deal, a was and now price
 
boosted odds, a price boost, a free bet or a welcome package in betting copy
 
offer terms missing, in small print below the price, or on screen too briefly to read
 
a price in the voiceover that differs from the price in the super
 
a promotion that may end before the campaign's last booked spot

3. What the executive checks
For a price or an offer, the Clearance Executive checks, in this order:
1
List every price, saving and offer in the copy, and where each appears: voiceover, super or end frame.
2
Check each offer's significant conditions sit with its headline and stay on screen long enough to read.
3
Ask for the pricing history behind any saving, to show it is genuine against the usual price.
4
Check the promotion runs for the whole booking, so that no spot advertises an offer that has ended.
5
For betting, check the minimum stake, the eligible markets and any wagering requirement are shown with the
offer.

4. Evidence to ask for
 
the full promotion terms
 
the pricing history for any saving or any was and now price
 
confirmation that the promotion runs for every booked spot
 
for betting, the wagering terms and the eligible markets

5. When the copy can be cleared
The copy can be cleared once each saving is shown to be genuine, every offer's significant conditions are legible
beside its headline, and the voiceover and the supers agree. The usual amendment is to enlarge the terms and hold
them for longer on the end frame, or to add the qualifying conditions beneath the headline.

6. What the agency should do
Before submitting, and when answering a query, the agency should:
 
Put the significant conditions beside the headline, not only in the small print.
 
Hold the terms on screen long enough to be read, at a size that can be read.
 
Keep the price in the voiceover and the price in the supers the same.
 
Send the pricing history and the full terms with the copy.

7. When to ask for a legal review
Ask for a legal review when an offer's conditions are complex, when a saving depends on a comparison with another
price, or when a betting offer carries a wagering requirement.
The Legal Adviser records the review on the campaign, and its view carries more weight than any other note.

8. Recording the outcome
The outcome is recorded in an update on the campaign: the copy amended, the evidence accepted, or the copy
cleared as submitted.
The assessment then recommends one of the decisions open for the campaign, and a Clearance Controller decides,
as the Advertising Clearance Policy describes. Copy that cannot be cleared is rejected, whatever its spots' results.

1. About this casebook
Eight closed campaigns, one for each copy issue, kept as worked examples of the Advertising Clearance Policy and
the category codes in practice. Each records the copy issue and how it was settled, how the booked spots were
checked against the category's code, and the decision.
The casebook is confidential. It records how other advertisers' campaigns were decided, is for Clearance Executives
and Clearance Controllers only, and is never quoted to agencies.
Each case applies the code of its own category. A figure quoted in one case belongs to that case's category and to
no other, and a campaign is always checked against the current code of its own category.

Brightkite Media. Medicines and health, pain relief. 18 spots booked on Harbourlight One and Harbourlight Life.
The first read questioned the line 'targets pain at the source', a claim about what the product does. The agency
changed the line to the wording the product's licence supports, and the revised copy was cleared.
Every spot met the medicines and health code. One was booked into the end break at 08:30 on Thursday on
Harbourlight Life, between Junior Newsdesk, a programme made for children, and Home Kitchen. The medicines
and health code forbids spots in a

and health code forbids spots in a programme made for children but not next to one, and neither programme was
forecast at an under-18 index of 150 or more, so the spot was cleared.

1. Purpose
These rules say how Harbourlight's schedule is read when a campaign's booked spots are checked against a
category code: the broadcast day and its clock, where a break sits, what in and adjacent mean, what live sport
coverage is, what the forecast under-18 audience index is and who publishes it, and how the daily limit and the
separation are counted.
They apply to all four channels and to every code.

2. The broadcast day and the booking week
Harbourlight's broadcast day runs from 06:00 to 05:59 the next morning. Every schedule, every count and every
comparison in a clearance is made on the broadcast day.
A booking covers one booking week of seven broadcast days, named Monday to Sunday. Days are named by
weekday only, and no clearance depends on a calendar date.
The small hours of Monday morning, before 06:00, belong to Sunday's broadcast day, not to the booking week's
Monday, which opens at 06:00.

3. The broadcast clock
Times on the broadcast day are written on the broadcast clock: 06:00 to 23:59 as usual, then 24:00 to 29:59 for the
hours after midnight, so the day runs in one direction from start to finish. A programme ends at 30:00 at the latest,
when the next broadcast day opens.
A time on the ordinary clock is moved onto the broadcast clock with one rule. A time from 06:00 belongs to the
broadcast day of its own weekday and keeps its clock. A time before 06:00 belongs to the previous weekday's
broadcast day, 24 hours later on its clock.
So Sunday 05:40 on the ordinary clock is Saturday 29:40, Saturday 23:10 stays as it is, and Monday 01:10 is Sunday
25:10, because the booking

ordinary clock is Saturday 29:40, Saturday 23:10 stays as it is, and Monday 01:10 is Sunday
25:10, because the booking week's Monday opens at 06:00.
A programme's end time at or before 06:00 on the ordinary clock is 24 hours later too. A programme from 23:30 to
00:30 runs from 23:30 to 24:30, and one from 05:30 to 06:00 on Sunday runs from Saturday 29:30 to 30:00.

4. How each channel writes the time
Harbourlight Sport's scheduling system, TXLine, writes the broadcast clock on the broadcast day: a spot at ten past
one on Sunday morning is written as Saturday 25:10. TXLine never writes a time before 06:00.
The systems of the other three channels - Airtime Planner for Harbourlight One, SlotMaster for Harbourlight Drama
and Planit for Harbourlight Life - write the ordinary clock on the calendar day, so the same spot is written as Sunday
01:10.
Each system also writes weekdays and spot lengths in its own way. A spot's length is always one of the standard
lengths, and the last three digits of its clock number give the length in seconds. Where the length

one of the standard
lengths, and the last three digits of its clock number give the length in seconds. Where the length written and the
clock number disagree, the clock number is right, because it identifies the copy.

5. Restricted hours on the broadcast day
A code writes its restricted hours on the ordinary clock. On the broadcast day they are placed with the same rule:
hours from 06:00 keep their clock, and hours before 06:00 move 24 hours later. Restricted hours that begin before
06:00 therefore fall in two parts of the broadcast day, one at its start and one at its end.
For example, hours written as 05:00 to 20:00 cover 06:00 to 20:00 and 29:00 to 30:00 of the broadcast day.
A break at the time restricted hours begin is inside them, and a break at the time they end is outside them. A break at
20:00 is clear of hours ending at 20:00, and a break at 05:00 is inside hours beginning at 05:00.

6. Where a break sits
Every spot is booked into a break, named by the time the break starts.
A break strictly inside a programme - after it starts and before it ends - is a centre break, and a spot in it is in that
programme.
A break at the moment one programme ends and the next begins is an end break, and a spot in it is adjacent to both
programmes, the one before and the one after.
No break is placed at the very start or the very end of the broadcast day, or in a gap in the schedule. A booking into
any of them is refused, not moved to the nearest break.

7. Live sport coverage
A programme the schedule marks as live sport is live sport coverage from its start to its end. Each live sport
programme is its own coverage, beginning and ending with the programme, even when another live sport programme
comes straight before or after it.
A centre break of a live sport programme is within the coverage. An end break is never within live sport coverage,
even between two live sport programmes.
Minutes after the coverage starts are counted from the programme's start to the break, and minutes before it ends
from the break to the programme's end. A break at 19:25 in coverage from 19:00 to 21:00 begins 25 minutes after the
coverage starts and 95 minutes

end. A break at 19:25 in coverage from 19:00 to 21:00 begins 25 minutes after the
coverage starts and 95 minutes before it ends.
Studio programmes about sport - previews, highlights, results and magazine programmes - are not live sport
coverage, even when they are broadcast live.

8. Programmes made for children
A programme is made for children when the schedule marks it so. The mark is set when the programme is
commissioned and does not depend on its audience: a programme made for children stays so whatever its forecast
index, and a programme with a high index is not made for children unless it is marked.

9. The forecast under-18 audience index
Harbourlight's audience planning team publishes a forecast under-18 audience index for every programme in the
booking week before the week begins, and the programme schedule carries it.
The index compares the share of a programme's audience expected to be under 18 with the share of under-18s in
the viewing population. An index of 100 means the programme is expected to draw under-18s in the same proportion
as the population, 200 twice that proportion and 50 half of it.
An index is a whole number from 1 to 999.
Clearance always uses the published forecast. The audience measured after a programme has aired is never used
to clear or withdraw a spot, and a

published forecast. The audience measured after a programme has aired is never used
to clear or withdraw a spot, and a revised forecast applies only once it is published in the schedule.

10. Counting the daily limit
A code's daily limit is counted per campaign, per channel and per broadcast day. The campaign's spots on that
channel in that broadcast day are counted in the order they are transmitted, earliest first, and every spot beyond the
limit breaks it.
Every booked spot counts, whether or not it breaks another rule. Two spots of one campaign in one break are
transmitted in the order of their spot references.
With a limit of four, for example, the fifth spot of the broadcast day and every spot after it break the limit, and a spot at
01:10 on Sunday morning counts towards Saturday's broadcast day.

11. Measuring the separation
A code's separation is measured from the campaign's previous spot on the same channel in the same broadcast day,
whatever that spot's own result. A spot that begins less than the separation after the previous spot breaks the rule; a
spot exactly the separation after it does not.
Times are measured between the breaks the spots are booked into, so spots at 20:20 and 20:35 are 15 minutes
apart, and two spots of one campaign in one break are zero minutes apart.
The first spot of a broadcast day on a channel has no previous spot, and a spot is never measured against one on
another channel or in another broadcast day.

12. How the results are recorded
Every spot is tested against every rule of its category's code. A spot that breaks no rule is compliant. A spot that
breaks any rule is recorded against every rule it breaks, in this order: restricted hours (WINDOW), the under-18
audience (INDEX), programmes made for children (CHILDREN), the daily limit (FREQUENCY) and the separation
(SEPARATION).
A spot's result never depends on whether another spot complies. The daily limit and the separation count and
measure every booked spot, whatever its own result.
